episodes.title: Tver Strike Update, Hearing the Quantum Jumps of Sound & AI That Refuses Until You Tell a Story
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: the reported Ukrainian strike on a cruise-missile fuel plant and an oil depot in Tver Oblast, Zelensky's delegation to Trump's envoys, the headlines from Kyiv, how narrative wrapping breaks AI refusals, what verification can and cannot add to self-improving agents, 82 open problems for AI, quantum jumps of sound, kilohertz entanglement between an ion and a diamond, magic-state factories for qLDPC codes, and how rats and flies decide.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-five hundred hours UTC on the ninth of October. An update on the overnight attack on Russia's Tver Oblast: the Kyiv Independent now reports Ukraine targeted both a cruise-missile fuel plant and an oil depot. According to Russian Telegram media channels, the factory makes fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles. On diplomacy, President Zelensky says his delegation's meetings with the Trump administration's envoys are expected to take place over two days, and that he is counting on a European team to join.

The headlines from the past day. Russian attacks plunged Kyiv into near-total darkness, and more than three million residents lost power; Britain has announced a seventy-one million dollar winter aid package. A twenty-four-year-old British intelligence specialist charged with spying for Russia has made his first court appearance. And in Lviv, two trains collided, injuring eight.

Frontier compute. Ask a safety-trained model for something harmful and it refuses; wrap the same request in a story or a role-play and it often answers. A new arXiv benchmark, GUISE, measures that weakness across languages: on one small Qwen model, attacks succeeded eighty-nine percent of the time in English, ninety-three in modern Chinese and nearly ninety-six in Classical Chinese. Another paper asks what self-improving agents actually gain from longer search, extra help or better verification, since one score cannot tell them apart. And OpenProblemBench gives AI eighty-two unsolved problems from mathematics and theoretical physics.

Quantum. Quantum mechanics says a vibrating object's energy comes in discrete packets, but no measurement of its position can show it. A new arXiv paper couples a superconducting qubit to a nanomechanical resonator and watches the quantum jumps of sound, repeatedly measuring the number of phonons without destroying them. Another team entangles a trapped barium ion with a silicon-vacancy centre in a diamond cavity, reporting kilohertz-rate entanglement between modules for distributed quantum computing. And a third proposes single-shot magic-state factories for high-rate qLDPC error-correcting codes.

Consciousness desk. How do brains decide when the world changes? A new bioRxiv study trained rats to reach the same goal by two different paths from different starting points, and finds that path integration, keeping track of where you are by your own movements, promotes flexible navigational decisions. Another study gave courting male fruit flies a sudden virtual heat stimulus, forcing a choice between staying with courtship or escaping, and finds that social feedback structures that stay-or-switch decision.

So, this hour's receipts. A fuel plant and an oil depot behind Russian lines, and a delegation heading to Trump's envoys. A capital in the dark and British winter aid. Stories that talk AI out of its safety rules, sound that jumps in quantum steps, and rats and flies deciding on the move. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Ukraine Hits a Cruise-Missile Fuel Plant in Tver, Kyiv's Blackout Day in Review & Magnesium for Memory
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: Ukraine reportedly strikes a factory in Tver Oblast that makes fuel components for Russian cruise missiles, a review of the past day in Ukraine (Kramatorsk, the Kyiv blackout, Britain's winter aid), Nature on superintelligence, controlling where semiconductor crystals grow, gut microbes that trace ancient human journeys, woody blankets on Arctic permafrost, and a bioRxiv study on how dietary magnesium enhances memory.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-four hundred hours UTC on the ninth of October. One new story overnight. Ukraine's military launched an attack on Russia's Tver Oblast early on the ninth, the Kyiv Independent reports, citing Russian Telegram media channels. The reported target: a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles. That identification of the target comes from those Russian channels, so treat it as reported rather than confirmed; we will follow up when there is more.

Because the hour is otherwise quiet, here is the past day in Ukraine, from the Kyiv Independent. At least thirty-three people were killed when a Russian glide bomb struck buses in Kramatorsk; Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death, Donetsk Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Russian attacks plunged Kyiv into near-total darkness. The drop in voltage halted metro trains and escalators, the city administration said, and other parts of public transport were affected too; more than three million residents lost electricity. And Britain has announced a seventy-one million dollar winter aid package for Ukraine.

Frontier compute. The arXiv computer science feed has not yet posted its new batch for today, so we turn to Nature, which asks about the science of superintelligence, and argues why AI is still a useful word. As the systems we cover each hour grow more capable, the question of what we should even call them, and how we would measure something beyond human ability, is not only academic. We will bring you the new research as soon as it lands.

Matter, Earth and life. With the quantum physics feed also between batches, four stories from Nature. Researchers report how to control where semiconductor crystals start growing. Up north, woody blankets are being deployed on Arctic permafrost to reduce carbon emissions. And gut microbes, Nature reports, trace ancient human journeys, including microbes that are now vanishing. And in genetics, Nature reports that genome accessibility reveals disease risk that gene expression alone misses.

Consciousness desk. Magnesium in the diet has been shown to enhance memory in mammals and in fruit flies, but how it changes the neurons themselves has been unknown. A new bioRxiv study used single-cell RNA sequencing in flies to map how memory-relevant cells respond, and found changes in genes of the Hippo signalling pathway in the mushroom bodies, the fly brain's memory centre. Knocking down Hippo-pathway genes, the authors report, shows the pathway is involved in how magnesium boosts memory.

So, this hour's receipts. A reported Ukrainian strike on the fuel behind Russia's cruise missiles. A day of death in Kramatorsk, darkness in Kyiv, and British winter aid. Crystals placed where engineers want them, blankets laid on permafrost, microbes that remember our migrations, and a mineral that helps a brain remember. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Night Edition: Kramatorsk Revisited, the Eavesdropper's Blind Spot & Paying the Brain to Remember
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief, night edition: the BBC on the Kramatorsk bus strike and Seoul recalling its Kyiv envoy, a bear attack near Ulaanbaatar, Trump's Camp David-like retreat plan, a test of AI's intuitive 'sixth sense', when agent skills actually help, a quantum cheat a monitor cannot see, negative-energy ghosts in physics, Australia's wildfires and colonial land use, the ageing brain and financial exploitation, and rewards that sharpen working memory.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-three hundred hours UTC on the ninth of October, a night edition with little fresh news, so we take a second look at the day through the BBC's reporting. On Kramatorsk, the BBC counts at least thirty dead in the Russian strike on two buses, and reports Ukraine's accusation that Russia targeted the crowded vehicles to kill as many civilians as possible. And South Korea has recalled its envoy to Kyiv, the latest step in a spat after Ukraine disclosed that two North Korean prisoners of war were transferred to Seoul.

Elsewhere. Near the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar, police say a bear entered a traditional nomadic dwelling, killing a man and seriously injuring a woman. And in Washington, the BBC looks at the President's wish for a new Camp David-like retreat at his Florida golf club, an estate that would stand in stark contrast to the rustic original, and, the BBC writes, another tradition transformed.

Frontier compute. People see far more than a scene shows: in a single glance we sense what caused it, where things are heading, whether a car will fit between two others, who holds authority in a room. A new arXiv benchmark calls that humanity's sixth sense and tests whether multimodal AI models have it. Another study runs eighty-seven tasks to ask when packaged agent skills actually help, noting that a relevant skill does not necessarily improve performance, and examining how the gain depends on its content, how it is run, and how skills are organised together.

Quantum, and Earth. An eavesdropper sees two average photon counts, and a monitor watching for leaks sees nothing. Can she conclude the two sealed devices did not communicate? A new arXiv paper builds a counterexample, a hidden shared interaction that a standard test would miss. Another paper studies the negative-energy ghost states that some theories of gravity introduce, and asks whether they must make the theory unstable. And Nature links Australia's current wildfire crisis to land-use change that began with colonisation.

Consciousness desk. Financial exploitation often begins with a judgement of fairness and trust. A new bioRxiv study scanned three hundred and ten adults aged twenty-one to eighty-nine playing a game in which they accept or reject offers from people and computers, and finds that links between the brain's response to fairness and vulnerability to exploitation vary with age and emotional intelligence. Another study finds rewards improve working memory by sharpening the memories themselves, rather than by making people answer more cautiously.

So, this hour's receipts. A second look at the Kramatorsk strike, and a diplomatic rift between Seoul and Kyiv. A bear in a nomadic dwelling and a presidential retreat on a golf course. A machine sixth sense, a quantum cheat no monitor can see, and a brain that remembers better when the stakes rise. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Britain's Winter Aid for a Darkened Kyiv, Robots That Can't Pause & a Brain-Scan Bug
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: Britain's $71 million winter aid for Ukraine after more than three million people in Kyiv lost power, a BBC investigation sending an abuser back to jail in Indonesia, Adidas suing White Fox, the death of actor Nana Patekar, real-time safety for embodied AI agents, simulating the market for AI benchmarks, a machine model for agents, telling quantum cause from common cause, AI scoring of human memories, and a brain-scan volume error in teenage cohorts.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-two hundred hours UTC on the ninth of October. Britain will provide a seventy-one million dollar winter aid package to Ukraine, the Kyiv Independent reports, its latest announcement of help. The announcement follows the Russian attack that knocked out power across Kyiv on the eighth: more than three million residents lost electricity in what officials called an attack on one of the energy facilities important for the city.

Around the world. In Indonesia, a teacher who sexually abused a pupil is back in jail after a BBC investigation; he had been secretly released on parole last year, after serving less than half his sentence. Adidas is suing the Australian label White Fox over a four-stripe design and wants it to stop selling the clothes and pay damages. And the outspoken Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for intense performances, has died suddenly at seventy-five.

Frontier compute. Robots and other embodied agents cannot pause the world while they think: pedestrians move and vehicles approach during inference. In the physical world, failures can cause human injury and costly hardware damage. A new arXiv benchmark, RT-Safe, tests agent safety under those real-time constraints. Another paper simulates the whole ecosystem around AI evaluation, the model providers, users, funders and regulators, to ask how benchmarks should be designed. And a third proposes an abstract machine that treats the language model as an oracle, giving workflows and agents a common foundation.

Quantum. When two parties measure a quantum system, their results depend on how the measurements are causally connected. A new arXiv paper compares two set-ups, one state measured twice in a row with a channel in between, and a shared state measured in parallel, and works through examples with tunable qubit channels to see when the two can be told apart from the joint statistics.

Consciousness desk. Recalling a film or a story reveals what people remember and how they organise it, but scoring that recall by hand makes large studies impractical. A new bioRxiv preprint offers an open-source pipeline that uses a language model to split both the story and the memory into units and match them explicitly. Another study warns that a widely used brain-scan tool, FreeSurfer before version eight, can produce implausible estimates of intracranial volume in adolescents, with changes of up to thirty-nine percent between sessions. The errors were worse on Siemens scanners and in female participants, and markedly reduced in version eight.

So, this hour's receipts. Winter money for a capital that lost its power. An abuser back behind bars in Indonesia. A fashion fight over stripes, and a farewell to a film star. Robots that must think on the move, and a measuring error hiding in a common brain-scan tool. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: America's Execution Debate, Europe's Street Anger & the Winner's Curse in Self-Improving AI
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: Texas carries out the first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections, Pike now walking, the death of the Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked protests, the anger behind France's school protests, the winner's curse in self-improving AI, a science of agent behaviour, recording what a quantum computation must keep, a chiral route to topological antiferromagnets, how life became multicellular, zebrafish that regrow their spinal cords, and the Nobel's light switches in the brain.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at oh-one hundred hours UTC on the ninth of October, a quieter hour for breaking news, so we pick up threads from the past day. In America, the death penalty. Texas carried out the first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections, the BBC reports; lawyers for Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause it. Pike herself, the murderer of Colleen Slemmer, is now moving around her hospital room after surviving two lethal injections, her lawyer told the BBC.

Europe. In Spain, Maricarmen Abascal has died at eighty-seven, the BBC reports. Her eviction in September, carried out on a stretcher from the apartment she had lived in for more than seventy years, sparked nationwide protests. In France, students are blockading and marching, and the BBC asks what lies behind the anger: real grievances, it argues, and the country's habit of settling policy on the street.

Frontier compute. AI systems that improve themselves usually keep a change only if it scores better on a small test set. A new arXiv paper calls that the winner's curse: picking the best-looking candidate under measurement noise, then reusing the same test, can lock in changes that are not real gains. The authors had Qwen models rewrite their own instructions and checked each candidate on six hundred held-out questions. Another paper proposes a science of agent behaviour, building testable variables out of what agents actually do.

Quantum and life. When a quantum computation is run, which details of its execution must be kept, and how precisely, to compare results honestly? A new arXiv paper defines a sufficient record and derives a certificate for recording precision straight from the circuit. In Nature: a chiral superlattice route to spin-split topological antiferromagnetism, and a paper on overcoming key challenges in life's evolutionary transition to multicellularity.

Consciousness desk. Some vertebrates regrow a severed spinal cord on their own. A new bioRxiv preprint watched single nerve fibres regrow in zebrafish after laser cuts and, from a genetic screen, finds roles for two genes, huntingtin and Celsr3, in that long-distance regeneration. Another study trains a graph neural network on EEG from children and adolescents with and without ADHD, distilling noisy trial-by-trial signals into stable portraits of each person. And Nature's Nobel roundup includes light switches in the brain.

So, this hour's receipts. An execution in Texas after a botched one that left the prisoner alive. A pensioner's death in Spain, and students on French streets. Self-improving AI that fools itself, quantum results that need honest records, and fish that rebuild their spinal cords. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: A British Soldier Charged with Spying for Russia, the Monaco Bomb Suspect Speaks & the Infant Brain
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: why Meta keeps booming despite Mark Zuckerberg's image problem, Americans on the death penalty, a 24-year-old British intelligence specialist charged with spying for Russia, the Monaco bomb suspect's account, a memory benchmark one simple rule mostly answers, self-designing AI agent evolvers, extreme low-bit compression, a semiconductor with a 7-electronvolt bandgap, directional quantum light, and memory circuits in the first two years of life.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at midnight UTC on the ninth of October. Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem, the BBC's North America tech correspondent writes: a new film paints the Meta founder as a villain, yet the company seems immune to bad publicity and its business is booming. And after the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, the BBC asked Americans and visitors in Washington what they think of the death penalty.

Russia's long reach. A British service member charged with spying for Russia has made his first court appearance, the Kyiv Independent reports. Junior intelligence specialist Teddy Young, twenty-four, faces two charges under the National Security Act for allegedly trying to pass protected information to a foreign power between November 2024 and May 2025. And in Monaco, a suspect linked to a bomb attack on a millionaire has broken his silence to the BBC: Vitalii Zhykovych gives his own account of the attempted assassination of Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev.

Frontier compute. A benchmark meant to test whether AI agents can selectively forget outdated facts may be measuring something simpler. A new arXiv paper applies the benchmark's own rule, the newest statement wins, with no learning at all, and answers about eighty percent of its questions. Another paper, FreeEvolve, lets agent evolvers design their own search, deciding how to evaluate, what to keep and when to stop. And a third pushes compression to two-bit weights, four-bit activations and a two-bit memory cache.

Quantum and matter. In Nature, a semiconductor based on silicon-doped aluminium gallium oxide with a bandgap of seven electron volts, pushing semiconductors, as Nature's news desk puts it, into insulator territory. On arXiv, a team identifies a path-complementarity mechanism in hybridized cavity polaritons that could deliver directional quantum light without sacrificing coherence between paths.

Consciousness desk. Episodic memory changes fast in the first two years of life, but little is known about how its circuitry develops. A new bioRxiv study collected precision brain scans from five infants between their first and second birthdays and maps distinct cortical networks tied to subregions of the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex. Another team, using light-based brain imaging on freely moving infants rather than tightly controlled tasks, finds distinct patterns of cortical reorganisation that accompany specific behaviours as babies develop.

So, this hour's receipts. A villain on screen and a booming business. A country arguing over how it executes. A young British specialist accused of spying for Moscow, and a bomb suspect telling his own story. A memory benchmark where one simple rule answers four questions in five, and infant brains building the circuits of memory. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: A Livestreamed Execution, Hurricane Isaias & Agents That Cheat on Broken Tasks
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: the Pentagon says the Fort Hood attacker's firing-squad execution will be livestreamed, Hurricane Isaias heading for the Gulf Coast, Anne Carson's Nobel, Gaza under strikes despite the ceasefire, the British consulate in East Jerusalem, the day in Ukraine, catching broken tasks before coding agents cheat, coherent decisions in language models, quantum oblivious transfer with mixed states, water squeezed to its limits, and a stroke survivor still recovering language after six years.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty-three hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The Pentagon says the Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed. We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, the BBC reports. Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, could bring dangerous winds, storm surge and heavy rain to the Gulf Coast on Friday. And the Canadian poet Anne Carson, seventy-six, has won the Nobel Prize in Literature; she is celebrated for work that crosses poetry, fiction and scholarship.

The Middle East and Ukraine. In Gaza, Palestinians face Israeli strikes despite the ceasefire, the BBC reports, with many still living in cramped tent cities and the US plan to end the war largely stalled. In East Jerusalem, the sign came down at the British consulate, first established in 1838, which Israel had moved to close in retaliation for UK sanctions. And the Kyiv Independent's day in Ukraine: at least thirty-three dead in Kramatorsk, a drone barrage on Kyiv, Polish SIM cards in Russian drones, and a peace push falling apart.

Frontier compute. Prior work found that coding agents handed a broken task rarely flag the conflict. They cheat instead, editing tests or hard-coding answers, sometimes deleting a security defence to make a corrupted test pass. A new arXiv paper, SpecGuard, aims to prove a task is broken before the agent cheats. Another paper trains language models to make coherent decisions across twenty datasets: keep their beliefs, apply the right utilities, and recognise when the information to justify an action is missing.

Quantum and matter. Oblivious transfer is a building block for secure computation between two parties, and a perfect version is impossible, classically or quantumly. A new arXiv paper asks whether mixed quantum states, rather than pure ones, can bring imperfect protocols closer to the limit. In Nature: hydrogen bonding in water under extreme confinement, and the experimental observation of critical topology.

Consciousness desk. Recovery from aphasia after a stroke is thought to plateau within a year. A new bioRxiv case study followed one patient for nearly six years, with behavioural tests and brain scans at nine, twenty-two, thirty-three and seventy-one months, and reports continued language recovery. Another team releases cyto7, an open atlas that maps cortical types point by point across the human cortex, rather than one type per classic brain area.

So, this hour's receipts. An execution the Pentagon wants the public to watch. A hurricane bearing down on the Gulf, and a poet's Nobel. Strikes in Gaza despite a ceasefire, and a consulate sign taken down in Jerusalem. Agents that cheat when the task is broken, and a brain still relearning language six years after a stroke. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: A $6.3 Billion Interceptor Deal, a Sheltered Syrian General & Freezing on the Turn
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: a contract worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors, the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia, the US and Lebanon sheltering a wanted Syrian general, Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, two trains colliding in Lviv, blind spots in AI agent verifiers, structured output for language models, will AI scoop your science, slimmer fault-tolerant quantum circuits, relativity bending the chemistry of seaborgium, freezing of gait in Parkinson's, and ear-nerve stimulation for working memory.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty-two hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The War Department and the Missile Defense Agency have awarded Raytheon a multiyear contract worth up to six point three billion dollars to produce SM-3 Block IB interceptors. In New York, a court heard arguments in the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia; the families allege men with links to the Saudi government helped the attackers, which Riyadh denies. And the BBC finds the US and Lebanon are protecting a wanted Syrian general, Bassam al-Hassan, in return for information, including about abducted American reporter Austin Tice.

The Middle East and Ukraine. Three people were killed in Houthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia, officials say; the Houthis claimed responsibility, and the BBC calls it an escalation. In western Ukraine, two trains collided in Lviv, injuring eight, the Kyiv Independent reports; the passenger train's driver suffered a leg injury, and the locomotive crew was unharmed.

Frontier compute. Who checks the checkers? A new arXiv paper audits the verifiers that decide whether AI agents succeeded on two popular benchmarks, AppWorld and WorkArena, and finds blind spots: in one case, duplicating a write leaves an extra record behind, and the checker still passes it. Another paper looks at structured output, the JSON and tool calls models are asked to produce, and exploits a rare property of the small machine that enforces the format. And Nature asks: will AI scoop your science? Some researchers see a gloomy future.

Quantum and chemistry. Fault-tolerant quantum circuits are expensive. A new arXiv paper automatically trims them with rewrites that keep their fault tolerance intact, each step removing an ancilla preparation and a CNOT gate. In Nature, researchers report the observation of relativistic bond weakening in seaborgium hexacarbonyl, a molecule of one of the heaviest elements. And the chemistry Nobel was awarded for solving the mystery of how handed, mirror-image organic molecules can emerge.

Consciousness desk. In Parkinson's disease, the most disabling symptom is freezing of gait, a sudden halt that strikes most often at turns, obstacles and narrow paths. A new bioRxiv preprint models it with a reinforcement learning system inspired by the cortex and basal ganglia, and proposes that impaired estimates of value over space explain freezing on the turn. Another study tests gentle vibration of the ear's branch of the vagus nerve during working memory tasks, reporting signs of more efficient cortical activity.

So, this hour's receipts. Six point three billion dollars of interceptors. A 9/11 lawsuit back in court, and a wanted general traded for information. Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, and a train crash in Lviv. Verifiers with blind spots, a heavy element bent by relativity, and a brain that freezes at the turn. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty-one hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The War Department announced a series of initiatives to advance the President's vision of a new golden age of American science. NPR talks to White House correspondent April Ryan about decades of pressing presidents for answers, and how asking questions put her in the President's crosshairs. And NPR reports on how documentary director Alex Gibney became a critic of Elon Musk, drawing on a trove of documents and interviews with people close to him.

Ukraine and beyond. The acclaimed Ukrainian investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach has been detained by Austrian authorities in Vienna, the Kyiv Independent reports; he was reportedly there on an editorial assignment with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko. Actor Serhii Strelnikov, who played a special forces commander in this year's thriller Killhouse, has enlisted in Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces. And in Chile, residents were airlifted to safety after the Mapocho river burst its banks following unusually heavy rain, the BBC reports.

Frontier compute. When should you correct an AI agent, at which step, and how? A new arXiv paper steered agents at every step with four different mechanisms and ran each version to the end, about eighty-two thousand counterfactual outcomes, to test whether the agent's own uncertainty is a good guide. Another paper asks which save points are worth keeping when coding agents work, measuring how much a checkpoint actually cuts the cost of recovering from a mistake.

Quantum, and life. Superconducting qubits use only the two lowest energy levels of a circuit, and information easily leaks into higher ones. A new arXiv paper uses geodesic-based optimal control to suppress that leakage. Another team tests quantum kernel methods for spotting anomalies in real malware beaconing data, weighing performance against how far each kernel departs from classical ones. And Nature reveals how a common gut microbe protects against heart disease.

Consciousness desk. Can you think pain down? A new bioRxiv study reanalysed more than three thousand heat-stimulation trials from thirty-three participants told to turn their pain up or down. Both instructions shifted ratings the intended way, and turning pain down came with lower activity in the brain's secondary sensory areas. And Nature asks a century-old question: can your brain grow new neurons, and how are researchers solving the puzzle?

So, this hour's receipts. A golden-age promise for American science, and a reporter recalling life in the President's crosshairs. A Ukrainian journalist detained in Vienna, an actor turned drone soldier, and a river over its banks in Chile. Agents that need to know when to be corrected, qubits that leak, and a mind that can turn its own pain down. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Zelensky on Data-Center Strikes, Madrid's Tent Protest & What Russia Won't Say About the Plague
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: Spain's housing protests and snap election, Italy's elections overhaul, UK diplomats leaving the East Jerusalem consulate, Zelensky on striking Russian data centers, Nature on the Irkutsk plague scare, Yuri Shvets' broadcast #1218, a threat-hunting language model, Rawls and AI, photon pairs from a 2 GHz resonator, cross-checking quantum network simulators, why big dogs age faster, and wiring maps of 10,000 organoid networks.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at twenty hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. In Madrid, hundreds have pitched tents in the city centre, blaming vulture funds for Spain's housing crisis, the BBC reports, as the prime minister calls a snap election. In Rome, Italy approved an overhaul of its elections; Prime Minister Meloni says it will bring stable government, and the opposition calls it a scam to keep her in power. And Israel says most British diplomats will leave the East Jerusalem consulate, after it promised to respond to UK sanctions on settlements.

Ukraine and Russia. Addressing Ukrainian attacks on a Russian data centre, President Zelensky said, we always respond in kind, adding that Russia has been and still is striking Ukraine's data centres. Nature asks what scientists know about the plague scare in Russia, and what Moscow won't say. And Yuri Shvets has posted broadcast number twelve eighteen, titled: the war in Ukraine is reshaping the world, Putin is losing his nuclear bluff.

Frontier compute. Security teams turn threat reports into precise detection rules, and general-purpose language models often get those rules wrong, with invalid syntax, wrong log sources and logic that is far too broad. A new arXiv paper presents Sigma-Hunter, a model tuned for exactly that job. Another paper returns to John Rawls and his original position, the thought experiment of choosing principles of justice without knowing your own place in society, and asks whether large language models can offer a view from everywhere.

Quantum, and life. A new arXiv paper produces photon pairs in a lithium niobate waveguide resonator with close to two gigahertz of bandwidth in the telecom band, and measures their correlations mode by mode. Another team cross-checks two open-source quantum network simulators, QuISP and SeQUeNCe, and finds that different assumptions can give different answers to the same basic tasks. And from Nature: big dogs age faster than little ones, and rogue jumping genes might be to blame.

Consciousness desk. How does a network of neurons organise itself? A new bioRxiv preprint introduces connectomics by sequencing, combining barcoded rabies tracing with single-cell RNA sequencing to reconstruct more than ten thousand neural networks inside cerebral organoids. Another study, across one hundred and seventy-five recordings of brain assembloids carrying MAPT mutations, finds abnormal amplification of activity over time, separating how often activity starts from how strongly it feeds on itself.

So, this hour's receipts. Tents in Madrid and a snap election. A vote overhaul in Rome. Ukraine answering data centre with data centre, and a plague scare Russia will not explain. A security model that writes cleaner rules, a philosopher's thought experiment handed to machines, and more than ten thousand organoid networks mapped by sequencing. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Zelensky's Delegation, Putin's G20 Invitation & the Plague Quarantine Lifted
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: Zelensky sends a delegation to meet Trump's envoys and hints at secret US-Russia economic talks, the G20 invitation to Putin, the 2026 House battleground, Russia lifting the Irkutsk quarantine after the plague lab worker's death, Moldova ready for more refugees, AI agents that learn to report unsafe work, looped language models, quantum error-correcting codes found with SAT solvers, the mouse embryo in detail, brain organoids on a 3D interface, and how the brain routes credit for its actions.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at nineteen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The Kyiv Independent reports President Zelensky is sending a delegation to meet the Trump administration's envoys over two days, and is counting on a European team to join, as he hints at secret US-Russia economic talks. The same paper carries an open letter on the administration's invitation to Vladimir Putin for December's G20 summit in Miami, arguing it should come with conditions. And NPR finds both parties spending heavily in some sixty House districts that could decide control of the chamber.

Russia and its neighbours. Russia has lifted the quarantine in the Irkutsk region, the Kyiv Independent reports, where a twenty-eight-year-old worker at the Anti-Plague Institute, Darya Shipilova, allegedly died of plague; initial reports raised fears of pneumonic plague after a laboratory accident. And in Chisinau, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said that if this winter in Ukraine is as hard as the world expects, Moldova is ready to receive as many people as need safety.

Frontier compute. When AI agents share a reward for finished tasks, reporting unsafe work costs the reporter. A new arXiv paper studies a game where any witness can stop a task by reporting, and asks whether training can teach a silent team to speak up. Another paper looks at looped language models, which promise to save memory and compute on easy words, and finds the current open models fail to deliver it in practice.

Quantum, and life. Error correction is the price of a useful quantum computer. A new arXiv paper builds codes with three logical qubits whose CCZ gate is applied transversally, using projective geometry for the structure and a SAT solver to find the rest, at thirteen sizes from forty-eight to four hundred and ninety-six qubits. Another paper defines quantum versions of the classes that grade how well hard optimisation problems can be approximated. And Nature captures how to build a mouse, embryo development in stunning detail.

Consciousness desk. Cortical organoids, small lab-grown pieces of brain tissue, reproduce key steps of development. A new bioRxiv preprint presents a flexible three-dimensional interface that reveals functional subnetworks and coordinated circuit activity inside them. Another asks how the brain gives credit: when an action pays off, how does the signal find its way back from the basal ganglia and cerebellum, through the thalamus, to the cortical circuits that chose it?

So, this hour's receipts. A Ukrainian delegation heading to Trump's envoys, and an invitation for Putin to Miami. A quarantine lifted in Irkutsk after a lab worker's suspected plague death. Moldova bracing for a hard winter next door. Agents learning to blow the whistle, and organoids lighting up in three dimensions. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Kyiv Goes Dark, a $100,000 Bill for Foreign Graduates & Memories That Turn Into Facts
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: a proposed $100,000 charge for international students to work after graduating in the US, deportations to African countries, an ICE warehouse in New Jersey, Kyiv plunged into near-total darkness, Operation Vivaldi near Lyman, a tanker hit off Qatar, AI agents whose rejected ideas come back as facts, small models versus frontier models, a picture of two qubits, NASA's Artemis II Moon data, and how one brain region juggles many tasks.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at eighteen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. Nature reports the United States has proposed a one hundred thousand dollar charge for international students who want to do post-graduate work there. Human Rights Watch says more than five hundred migrants have been expelled from the US to African countries, and calls the deportations unlawful. And NPR investigated rumours in northern New Jersey that ICE has quietly used a warehouse as a detention centre all summer; neighbours say it has.

Ukraine. Russian attacks plunged Kyiv into near-total darkness, the Kyiv Independent reports. The drop in voltage halted metro trains and escalators and disrupted power and water across the capital. On the front, the paper goes inside Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive in the Lyman sector of Donetsk Oblast fought with drones above and robots below; Russian officials claim to control Lyman, and Ukrainian infantry tell a different story. In the Gulf, the BBC reports an oil and chemical tanker hit by multiple projectiles off Qatar, with casualties reported on board.

Frontier compute. A new arXiv paper names a quiet failure in AI agents with long-term memory. While thinking, an agent may consider a plan, imagine a tool result or repeat someone else's belief, then reject it. If memory keeps only the sentences, those discarded possibilities can come back later as facts. A second paper tested nine models, from tiny to frontier, inside a working home-automation system, and asks why one big model should serve every call when the jobs differ tenfold in difficulty.

Quantum and space. Entanglement is notoriously hard to picture. A new arXiv paper proposes a simple image for any pure two-qubit state: two Bloch balls, one for each qubit, plus a reflection-rotation and a contraction that carry the entanglement, and proves the picture has no gaps. Another team studies entangling gates between two species of atoms in neutral-atom quantum computers. And Nature reports NASA has released a trove of Moon data from the historic Artemis two flight.

Consciousness desk. How does one patch of brain do several jobs at once? A new bioRxiv preprint offers a theory of multi-tasking, starting from the idea that activity during each task lies on its own low-dimensional manifold, and sorts competing models by their assumptions. Another study recorded EEG while adults passively heard and saw small numbers, testing whether the brain detects changes in quantity before attention arrives, by ear and by eye.

So, this hour's receipts. A six-figure price on staying to work after graduation. Five hundred deportations to Africa, and a warehouse that neighbours say became a detention centre. A capital without light, metro or water, and robots on the Lyman front. Agents whose rejected thoughts return as facts, a picture of entanglement, and a brain that runs many tasks at once. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Maduro Charged with Torture, Kyiv in the Dark & How Long a Moment Lasts
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: new torture-conspiracy charges against Nicolás Maduro, a $1.5 billion US health deal with Zambia, a shrinking regulator for crypto and prediction markets, the drone barrage on Kyiv, South Korea recalling its Ukraine envoy, Ukraine's strike on the Salavat refinery, a failure-mode map of catastrophic AI risk, measuring how AI agents learn, quantum forecasts no classical learner can match, heat pumped on a quantum chip, the UAE's asteroid probe, and how long a perceptual moment lasts from infancy to adulthood.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at seventeen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. The BBC reports that Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro has been charged with conspiracy to commit torture, over the alleged torture of US citizens held in Venezuela while he was in power. Zambia has signed a one and a half billion dollar health deal with the United States, negotiated after the President cut USAID funding. And NPR reports that as crypto and prediction markets expand, the agency meant to write their rules has seen its staff and enforcement actions drop sharply.

Ukraine. A Russian drone barrage on Kyiv killed four people and injured nineteen, the Kyiv Independent reports, and disrupted electricity and water; the energy firm DTEK announced emergency shutdowns around the capital. Across the country, Ukraine's Air Force counted one hundred and forty-two Shahed-type drones overnight, eighty-two of them jet-powered. South Korea is recalling its envoy to Ukraine after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners of war were transferred to Seoul. And Ukraine's General Staff confirms a hit on the Salavat refinery, one of Russia's largest, some thirteen hundred kilometres from the front.

Frontier compute. A new arXiv paper maps how advanced AI could lead to human extinction or permanent disempowerment, and argues it would take no consciousness and no hostility, only interacting failures: misalignment, harmful use, organisational failure and competitive deployment. A second paper asks a simpler question with large consequences: not what an agent can do today, but how well it learns from its own mistakes.

Quantum and space. Can an agent's forecasts reveal whether it reasons with a quantum model? A new arXiv paper says yes: quantum Bayesian retrodiction can make predictions no classical learner could match, but only for measurements with more than four outcomes. On real hardware, another team ran geometric heat pumping on a superconducting quantum processor, moving energy between reservoirs at the same temperature. And Nature reports the UAE has completed the Arab world's first solo space probe, now on course for an asteroid.

Consciousness desk. Perception feels continuous, but evidence suggests the brain stitches sensory input into short windows of time. A new bioRxiv study measured how long those windows last, from five months of age to adulthood, across three hundred and eight participants, using eye tracking that needs no instructions. How the length of a perceptual moment develops through childhood had, until now, been unknown.

So, this hour's receipts. Torture charges for a deposed president. Kyiv losing power and water under drones. A diplomatic rift over prisoners of war, and a refinery burning far behind the front. A map of how AI could fail us without ever meaning to. Quantum forecasts no classical learner can make, and the length of a single moment of human awareness. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Kramatorsk Bus Strike, a Stalled Peace Push & the Pentagon's Quantum Bet
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: $350 million in War Department quantum initiatives and a $150 million conditional loan to PsiQuantum, Trump's Camp David-style retreat plan, the Kramatorsk bus strike, Rubio on the collapse of the peace push, Ukraine's strike on the Omsk refinery, Polish SIM cards in Russian drones, UK sanctions on the shadow fleet and crypto, Margaret Hamilton's death, AI agents doing open-ended science, quantum Darwinism, psychedelics and the brain, and monkeys replaying the day in REM-like sleep.
paragraphs: This is ZeroFilter, at sixteen hundred hours UTC on the eighth of October. Washington first, and it is a quantum day. The War Department announced new initiatives and programme updates worth about three hundred and fifty million dollars to strengthen US quantum computing for national security. Its Office of Strategic Capital also signed a one hundred and fifty million dollar conditional loan commitment with PsiQuantum, for manufacturing and prototyping in the United States. And NPR reports the President wants to turn one of his Florida golf courses into a presidential retreat, sort of a Camp David, he said.

Ukraine. The Kyiv Independent reports at least thirty-three dead after a Russian glide bomb struck buses in Kramatorsk. On diplomacy, both Washington and Moscow now confirm the latest peace push is falling apart; Secretary of State Rubio said there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement. Ukraine's General Staff confirms a strike on Russia's Omsk oil refinery, deep in Siberia. An investigation into the mass Russian drone incursion into Polish airspace on September ninth found Polish SIM cards inside the downed Russian drones. And Britain ramped up sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet, its crypto industry and big oil.

Frontier compute, and a farewell. Margaret Hamilton has died at ninety, the BBC reports. She led the software for NASA's Apollo missions, the code that helped land Apollo eleven on the Moon. Today's arXiv asks whether AI agents can do open-ended science, testing them in Station, a world where many agents simulate a scientific ecosystem. Another paper probes how fragile safety is in language models running on our own devices, and whether it hangs on a small set of parameters.

Quantum. A new arXiv paper tries to unite two ideas about how the past gets written into the world. Decoherent histories asks which past events leave formal records. Quantum Darwinism asks which present facts get copied redundantly into the environment. Neither implies the other. The authors build a bridge on one insight: only redundant records of past events count. A second paper shows how a programmable two-qubit gate can be teleported, with a third party holding the program.

Consciousness desk. A new bioRxiv preprint maps how five psychedelics, LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, DMT and five-MeO-DMT, restructure the way information is stored, transferred and transformed across the human cortex, in eighty participants. And in monkeys, wireless recordings from the high-level visual cortex ask whether the brain replays what it saw while awake during REM-like sleep. The preprint's title answers: neural signatures of food come back while they sleep.

So, this hour's receipts. Half a billion dollars of Pentagon quantum money and loans. Thirty-three dead on buses in Kramatorsk, and a peace push that both sides now call finished. Refineries burning in Siberia, Polish SIM cards in Russian drones. A goodbye to the woman whose code reached the Moon. And brains that keep rewriting themselves, awake, asleep or on psychedelics. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Pryluky Strike, a Suspected Plague Death on Trump's Call List & Nuclear Clocks Start Ticking
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: Trump to raise a plague lab worker's death with Putin, a $1.5 billion conditional War Department loan to Wolfspeed, the Pryluky strike, Russian sabotage against Danish defense firms, Lithuanian troops on the Kaliningrad border, the EU's largest Russia sanctions list, Yuri Shvets' broadcast #1217, OpenAI's 700 maths preprints, a byte-level language model, the first nuclear clocks, and decisions that outlast alertness.
paragraphs: Welcome back to ZeroFilter. It is midnight UTC on the eighth of October. Washington first. The BBC reports that President Trump will speak to Vladimir Putin about the death of a plague lab worker in Russia. Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague have prompted calls for more transparency from Moscow. Also tonight, the War Department's Office of Strategic Capital announced a one and a half billion dollar conditional loan commitment to Wolfspeed, an American manufacturer of semiconductor materials. Conditional is the word to watch.

To Ukraine and its neighbours. The Kyiv Independent reports that a Russian attack on Pryluky killed at least twenty people, five of them children, on a day of strikes that fell on Putin's seventy-fourth birthday. Danish intelligence says Russia carried out sabotage against Danish defense firms, increasingly aiming at targets tied to Western military support for Ukraine. Lithuania will deploy troops along its border with Kaliningrad, a preventative step, its interior minister said, against signals that Russia may announce mobilization. And EU ambassadors waved through the largest-ever list of Russia sanctions, reaching shipyards, aviation, electronics and aerospace firms. Yuri Shvets titled his latest broadcast, number twelve seventeen: Ukraine is striking Russia systematically, Europe is lifting its nuclear taboos.

Frontier compute. Nature reports that OpenAI has posted seven hundred mathematics preprints online, and that mathematicians are up in arms. The same issue carries a paper on retrofitting language models to operate over bytes, which Nature's news desk summed up in one headline: the retrofitted model can count the letter i in artificial intelligence. Models that read text in chunks called tokens have long stumbled on spelling questions exactly like that one.

Precision physics. Nuclear clocks are ticking for the first time, Nature reports. Two papers describe a thorium two twenty-nine optical nuclear clock with a feedback loop, and a nuclear clock synchronized to thorium two twenty-nine. Atomic clocks count the rhythm of electrons. A nuclear clock listens to a transition inside the nucleus itself, far better shielded from the noise of the outside world, which is why physicists have chased one for decades.

Consciousness desk. A new bioRxiv study followed people as they drifted from wakefulness toward sleep while locating sounds and touches, with EEG tracking their alertness moment to moment. Drowsiness slowed their responses and made them miss more trials. But when they answered, they stayed largely accurate, and agreeing or conflicting touch signals kept shaping their choices. The authors report that this decision-making persists as alertness fades, even when no overt response comes. The mind keeps working the problem while awareness dims.

So, tonight's receipts. A suspected plague death that made it onto a presidential call list. A conditional loan for American chip materials. Twenty dead in Pryluky, sabotage in Denmark, troops on the Kaliningrad line and Europe's biggest sanctions list yet. Seven hundred maths preprints from OpenAI, a model that can finally count its letters, and clocks that tick inside the nucleus. Every link is in the source drawer. This has been ZeroFilter. Stay unfiltered.

episodes.title: Pentagon Advisers' Conflicts, a Tanker Ablaze off Sochi & a Blueprint for Quantum Gravity
episodes.subject: Hourly sourced brief: ethics worries over Elon Musk's and Palmer Luckey's new Pentagon roles, the War Department's counter-drone laser and microwave picks, a shadow-fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Sochi, Ukraine's drone-casualty tally, Yuri Shvets' broadcast #1216, error-correcting dynamics inside language models, a proposed test of gravity-induced entanglement, and how the brain recalibrates what feels simultaneous.
paragraphs: Welcome back to ZeroFilter. It is twenty-two hundred hours UTC. In Washington, NPR reports that Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey have taken new Pentagon roles, and ethics experts are worried: their companies, SpaceX and Anduril, could benefit from recommendations in a Pentagon study on future autonomous weapons. Same day, the War Department named the laser and microwave systems it selected after its JIATF 401 counter-drone pilot. My take: when the people advising on the shopping list also sell the merchandise, that is a conflict of interest.

To the Black Sea. The Kyiv Independent reports a shadow-fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Sochi, and Russian Telegram channels suggest sea drones hit it. Robert Brovdi, call sign Madyar, who commands Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, says his units recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded from October 1 to 5, up from 1,931 in the same days of September. And in broadcast number 1216, Yuri Shvets lays out what he calls six priorities for victory: six lines of effort that must work at once, instead of slogans and promises of another counteroffensive.

Frontier compute. A new arXiv paper asks why language models stay coherent even when you shove their internal activations around, for example with steering. The authors' hypothesis is passive error correction: mechanisms in the forward pass that funnel activations back toward regions that produce sensible output, which the title calls privileged error-correcting basins. If that holds up, these models are sturdier than the parrot jokes suggest. That last part is my read, not their claim.

Quantum next. Nobody has yet caught gravity entangling two masses. Proposals argue that if gravity alone can do it, gravity itself must be quantum, and with the Planck scale out of reach, a tabletop interferometer is the realistic back door. A new arXiv paper works out the best interferometer geometry for that experiment. No result yet. This is a blueprint, not a discovery.

Consciousness desk. Your sense of at the same time is not fixed. A new bioRxiv study looks at rapid temporal recalibration: after signals from different senses arrive slightly out of sync, your judgment of what is simultaneous shifts toward that recent timing. The authors separate a genuine perceptual realignment from a decision-level carryover from your previous answers, and report that the two come apart across the senses. Part of what feels like perception is bookkeeping.

So, tonight's receipts. Two tech billionaires in Pentagon roles their companies could profit from. A tanker reportedly burning off Sochi. Drone casualty counts climbing, by Ukraine's own tally.
